scenes.text: Under a microscope, a zebrafish embryo may look clear. But cutting a meaningful histological section begins long before the blade touches tissue.
The specimen's orientation matters. A small change in angle can place the brain, heart, or other anatomy outside the section you hoped to examine.
My approach used two percent agarose as a temporary support. It held the tiny zebrafish specimens in a chosen orientation for subsequent processing.
After dehydration and clearing, paraffin was supposed to provide the support needed for microtomy. Each material had a different task in the proposed sequence.
Then came the decisive moment. The agarose and paraffin did not behave as one coherent block: the interface separated when sectioning was attempted.
Instead of a ribbon of thin, interpretable tissue sections, fragments accumulated. These archival photographs document that result, not a successful histology slide.
The microtome did not establish the cause of the failure. The immediate observation was separation between the two materials during processing and sectioning.
Agarose is a water-loving gel; paraffin is hydrophobic. Their contrasting properties suggest an interface problem, but the exact mechanism was not demonstrated.
A different agarose grade or revised processing conditions could be tested. Those remain possibilities, not solutions verified by this experiment.
I kept the unsuccessful photographs. They show where a plausible method stopped yielding interpretable evidence. A failed preparation can still define a rigorous next question.
